We found that, on average, DENV3 in Asia resulted in the highest proportion of DHF/DSS (21·00% [95% CrI: 13·02–30·44%]) and hospitalised (22·00% [95% CrI: 0·88–75·31%]) cases among symptomatic primary infections, while also causing the highest proportion of DHF/DSS among secondary infections (37·61% [95% CrI: 24·19–52·32%]). However, conditional on the same prior exposure status (primary/secondary infections), we found no statistically significant differences between serotypes across the three severity definitions. For 1997-type severity, we found some evidence of secondary infections being more severe than primary infections and found that dengue was significantly less severe in the Americas when compared to Asia, though this disparity between regions was sensitive to the inclusion of cases with unknown prior exposure status. There was no significant difference between regions for 2009-type severity and hospitalisations. The paucity of published studies from Africa limited the extent to which we could investigate dengue severity in this region. Interpretation This study provides evidence that, according to the published literature, prior dengue exposure has a stronger association with the development of severe disease than the serotype of infection. Better characterising the local population-level immunity remains a current priority for outbreak response and healthcare demand planning. Funding UK Medical Research Council, UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, Wellcome Trust, European Union.

title: MGUS in Black individuals in Soweto, South Africa screened by mass spectrometry: results of the PROMISE South Africa study
abstract: Background Only few studies have screened for monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) among Black Africans in sub-Saharan Africa, with mixed results. Methods In this cross-sectional study, we enrolled 2004 Black Africans aged 40–75 years from Soweto, South Africa, from January 2021 to August 2023. Participants completed an interview-guided exposure survey, underwent height and weight measurements, and provided blood samples that were screened for MGUS by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionisation-time of flight mass spectrometry. The primary outcome was the prevalence of MGUS, assessed from blood samples collected at the participants' single study visit. Prevalence was compared to those of high-risk United States (US)-based cohorts screened by the same method. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated associations between exposures and MGUS. Findings Prevalences of heavy-chain and light-chain MGUS among Black Africans were 12% and 3%. MGUS prevalence among Black Africans were similar to or higher than those of high-risk populations in the US. In multivariable modelling within the South Africa cohort, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was associated with MGUS (odds ratio [OR], 1.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.27–2.21; p < 0.001). Smoking was associated with MGUS (<20 pack-years vs never smoking: OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14–2.12; p=0.01 and ≥20 pack-years vs never smoking: OR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.21–2.56; p=0.003). Body mass index (BMI) of ≥30 kg/m 2 (vs normal BMI) was inversely associated with MGUS (OR, 0.59; 95% CI, 0.40–0.85; p=0.01), as was high physical activity (≥52.5 vs <10.5 metabolic equivalent of task-hours/week: OR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.19–0.96; p=0.04). Interpretation Results suggest Black South Africans represent a high-risk population with an increased likelihood of having MGUS. HIV, smoking, and physical activity may contribute to prevalence patterns. Prospective studies are needed to further elucidate the role of these risk factors in MGUS development and to identify strategies for early detection, risk stratification, and prevention. Funding Stand Up To Cancer Dream Team, Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation, and National Institutes of Health.

title: Global burden of dengue on healthcare systems: a meta-analysis of healthcare resource utilisation
abstract: Background Dengue poses an increasing health challenge, yet contemporary global healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU) data remain limited. Methods A systematic literature review (SLR) and meta-analysis of studies published 2013–2026 was conducted to estimate hospitalisation rate (HR) and length of stay (LOS) for dengue. Pooled proportions and means were analysed with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) under fixed- and random-effects models globally and by region. Meta-regression models estimated potential sources of heterogeneity. Additionally, sensitivity (excluding sample sizes <100, >50,000, and >50,000 and <100) and subgroup analyses were conducted for disease severity, patient characteristics, and region (PROSPERO# CRD42023480948). Findings Of 341 studies included in the SLR, studies reporting HR (121) and LOS (204) were prioritised for analysis. Global HR among patients with dengue, irrespective of severity, was 36.7% (95% CI 29.0–44.4), under the random-effects model. HR was higher for severe versus non-severe dengue (79.4% [55.9–92.2] versus 26.6% [19.3–35.4]), with versus without warning signs (36.9% [23.3–52.9] versus 17.7% [10.2–28.9]), and in Asia versus Latin America (35.1% [18.0–57.2] versus 29.3% [18.4–43.2]). Global mean LOS among hospitalised patients with dengue, irrespective of severity, was 4.9 days (95% CI 4.6–5.2) under the random-effects model. Severe dengue had longer LOS versus non-severe dengue (6.5 [5.4–7.7] versus 4.6 [4.3–4.9] days), especially for patients with versus without comorbidities (6.1 [5.1–7.2] versus 5.1 [4.3–5.9] days), and in Asia versus Latin America (5.1 [4.8–5.5] versus 4.1 [3.4–4.7] days). Meta-regression showed disease severity was the single significant factor (p < 0.0001) associated with high HR and longer LOS (I 2 ≥ 99.8%) among the factors analysed. Interpretation Due to high heterogeneity between studies and interregional differences, pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution. These findings indicate the considerable burden of dengue driven by HCRU, offering valuable insights for health system preparedness, clinical trial design, and policy planning. Funding Novartis Pharma AG.

title: Gestational age references and trajectory of fetal haemoglobin in relation to outcome in neonates born before 30 weeks of gestation: a single-centre retrospective cohort study in The Netherlands
abstract: Background: Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) has a high oxygen affinity and predominates during fetal life. After birth, HbF is progressively replaced by adult haemoglobin (HbA). In preterm neonates, transfusion with HbA-containing red blood cells (RBCs) may accelerate this transition, increasing tissue oxygen exposure and oxidative stress, which have been associated with retinopathy of prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and necrotizing enterocolitis. We aimed to establish gestational age (GA)-specific reference values and examine postnatal HbF trajectories in relation to transfusion exposure and outcomes, focusing on neonates born before 30 weeks' gestation. Methods: In this single-centre retrospective cohort study, 856 neonates with HbF measurements (24-42 weeks' gestation) admitted to the ErasmusMC NICU, Rotterdam, the Netherlands (1 February 2020-1 February 2024) were included. GA-specific HbF reference values were derived from day 0 samples. Longitudinal HbF trajectories during NICU admission were analysed in 458 neonates born before 30 weeks' gestation using 9461 blood gas samples. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations between HbF decline, transfusion exposure, and prematurity-related outcomes. Findings: HbF at birth remained high until approximately 35 weeks' gestation (median ≥0.85) and declined towards term. In neonates born before 30 weeks' gestation, HbF declined during the first postnatal weeks, with the steepest decline seen in babies born at 24-25 weeks' gestation. Neonates who received RBC transfusions showed a steeper HbF decline than those who did not (p < 0.001), as did neonates with prematurity-related outcomes compared with those without major morbidity or mortality (p < 0.001). Interpretation: RBC transfusions accelerate HbF decline in neonates born before 30 weeks' gestation. Its association with prematurity-related morbidity supports evaluation of HbF-preserving transfusion strategies. Future studies should incorporate the interval and frequency of successive transfusions through time-varying cumulative transfusion exposure or analyses centred on individual transfusion events to further refine the temporal dynamics of HbF decline and recovery. These studies should ultimately evaluate the optimal interval and frequency of transfusions and whether HbF-preserving transfusion strategies improve clinical outcomes in extremely preterm neonates. Funding: No funding was received for this work.

title: A cross-sectional global policy analysis of the human gap in 156 national cancer strategy plans
abstract: Background: National Cancer Strategies (NCS), including National Cancer Control Plans (NCCPs) and Non-Communicable Disease Plans (NCDPs), shape priorities for cancer systems. Yet, little is known about whether they address human-centred care, including psychosocial support, equity, financial protection, and palliative care. We aimed to (1) assess the extent to which NCS include human-centred care themes relevant to sociocultural factors, systems of care, medical education, economic protection, mental health, and palliative care, and (2) compare inclusion across lower- and higher-income settings. Methods: The International Cancer Control Partnership, an initiative developed under the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC), maintains a database of NCS to facilitate cancer planning and policy development worldwide. Using the 2023 UICC global review questionnaire dataset, this secondary analysis examined 20 questionnaire items across 98 NCCPs and 58 NCDPs from 156 countries. Items were grouped into six themes relevant to human-centred care and analyzed by country income level. Findings: Only 12% of NCCPs identified people living with cancer as stakeholders. Most countries included strategies addressing palliative care beyond pain management (84%), and 72% included strategies to support families or caregivers of cancer patients. In contrast, few countries addressed social determinants of health (28%), cancer-related inequities (28%), protection against catastrophic expenditure (14%), or referenced essential medicines for psychological distress (3%). Human-centred care themes were less frequently addressed in lower-income settings compared with higher-income settings (32% vs. 44%). Interpretation: Themes of human-centred care are infrequently included in NCS, particularly in lower-income countries. Global attention to these themes is needed to advance more equitable, human-centred cancer care worldwide. Funding: None.

title: High-dose vitamin D3 supplementation in the prevention of viral-induced asthma in high-morbidity preschoolers (DIVA): a randomised controlled trial in Canada
abstract: Background: Systematic reviews have suggested a beneficial effect of vitamin D supplementation in reducing asthma exacerbations and respiratory infections, with an underrepresentation of individuals with severe asthma and preschoolers. We aimed to examine the efficacy and safety of high-dose vitamin D supplementation for reducing severe exacerbations in preschool-aged children with viral-induced, high-morbidity, and asthma. Methods: In this randomised, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, triple-blind, multicentre trial, children aged 1-5 years with prior viral-induced exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids (OCS) were enrolled across nine paediatric asthma centres in Canada. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either two oral boluses of 100,000 IU (3·5 months apart) with daily 400 IU vitamin D3, or placebo boluses and daily placebo, over 7 months. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations requiring rescue OCS during the 7-month follow-up, analysed by a negative binomial regression model. Secondary outcomes included laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections, health care utilisation, duration and severity of exacerbations, and safety. This trial was prospectively registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03365687). Findings: Between Sept 18, 2018, and April 22, 2024, 1072 children were screened. Due to pandemic-related recruitment constraints, the trial enrolled 323 children, representing 37% of the planned sample size of 865 children. Participants had a mean age of 2·8 years (65% male) with a median of 2 (interquartile range: 1-3) oral corticosteroid courses in the prior year; at baseline, 48% had baseline serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) ≥75 nmol/L and 90% received GINA 2024 Step ≥3 therapy. Compared to placebo, there was no significant group difference in the rate of rescue OCS per child (0·67 ± 0·94 vs. 0·71 ± 1·02, incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0·95; 95% CI 0·70-1·30), laboratory-confirmed infections (1·73 ± 1·71 vs. 1·76 ± 1·55, IRR 0·99; 0·82-1·21), acute-care visits, duration and/or severity of exacerbations, and treatment-emergent or serious adverse events adverse events. The intervention was associated with a rapid and sustained rise in 25(OH)D. Interpretation: In preschoolers with high-morbidity, viral-induced asthma, vitamin D3 supplementation did not significantly reduce severe exacerbation or respiratory viral infection rates, compared to placebo. No safety concerns were observed. With fewer participants than planned, the precision of estimates is limited and the results are inconclusive, thus deserve further exploration. Funding: Canadian Institutes of Health Research.

title: Associations of digital media use with health, behavioural and developmental outcomes in children and adolescents: an umbrella review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Digital media (screen) use is nearly universal among children and adolescents, yet evidence on its associations with health outcomes remains fragmented across exposure types and outcome domains. We aimed to synthesise review-level evidence and quantify associations between digital media use and health, behavioural and developmental outcomes across childhood and adolescence. Methods This systematic umbrella review (PROSPERO-CRD420251175522) includes systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses published from Jan-2021 to Dec-2025 that investigate digital media exposures and their associations with health, behaviour, and development among individuals aged 0–24. Evidence was synthesised narratively and quantitatively, and stratified according to developmental stage (mainly 0–10 & 10–24 years; additionally, subgroups aged 0–5, 5–10, 10–18, 18–24 years and others). Methodological quality and certainty of evidence were assessed using validated tools, and overlap of primary studies was assessed using corrected covered area analysis. Findings We included 121 systematic reviews (52 with meta-analyses), comprising 2790 unique primary studies and over 9 million participants. Quality assessment showed that approximately two-thirds of the available literature was rated as low/critically-low quality, largely reflecting the observational nature of the underlying evidence. Mental health accounted for the largest share of findings (36%), with the direction and magnitude of associations varying according to developmental stage and the type, content, context, and pattern of digital media use. In children aged 0–10 years, overall screen time was associated with poorer socio-emotional and cognitive development and shorter sleep duration, whereas educational content and caregiver co-viewing were associated with improved language and cognitive outcomes. In adolescents aged 10–24 years, problematic digital media use and social media use were associated with higher odds of common mental health problems, lower quality of life, sleep problems, reduced physical activity, self-harm or suicidal ideation, and substance use, while active video games and body-positive content were associated with higher well-being and physical activity. Physical-health outcomes, including obesity, myopia, and cardio-metabolic risk, were reported in samples spanning childhood to adolescence. Interpretation The health implications of digital media use varied across developmental stages and according to the amount, content, context, and patterns of exposure. Given the predominantly observational nature of the evidence, the findings should not be interpreted as causal. Strengthening causal inference through longitudinal and experimental studies, alongside objective exposure assessment and broader outcome evaluation, remains a key research priority. Funding This work was supported by funding from the National University of Singapore under the Academic Health Programme (AHP) through the POPUP project and PANDA Research Programme. The Digital Transformations for Health Lab supported costs associated with project management, coordination, and stipends for Youth Advisory Group members.

title: Prevalence and clinical course of pelvic pain among transmasculine individuals on gender-affirming testosterone: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background: Pelvic pain is increasingly recognised among transmasculine individuals receiving gender-affirming testosterone therapy, yet no systematic synthesis of prevalence or clinical course exists. Methods: We conducted the first systematic review and meta-analysis of pelvic pain in transgender individuals. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL from January 2013 to June 2026. Studies reporting prevalence or clinical course of pelvic pain in transmasculine individuals with or without testosterone therapy were included. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261278643. Findings: Eleven studies encompassing 4176 transmasculine individuals were included, of whom 2891 received testosterone therapy. Among those receiving testosterone, the pooled prevalence of pelvic pain was 39% (95% CI 23-55%), significantly higher than in cisgender women (5-25%). Prevalence was higher in surgical cohorts (50%, 95% CI 12-88%) than in non-surgical populations (28%, 95% CI 13-46%). New-onset pelvic pain was reported in 31% (95% CI 5-65%) of previously asymptomatic individuals after testosterone initiation. Critically, among individuals with preexisting pain, 72% (95% CI 62-81%) reported persistence, while only 26% (95% CI 18-34%) reported improvement or remission after testosterone initiation. Interpretation: Pelvic pain is common among transmasculine individuals and frequently persists despite testosterone therapy. These findings challenge the widespread assumption that androgenic hormonal transition is protective against pelvic pain and highlight the urgent need for proactive assessment and gender-affirming management in this population. Prospective studies with standardised pain assessment and investigation of hormonal, tissue-level, and psychosocial mechanisms are needed to develop evidence-based interventions. Funding: No funding was received.

title: Cost-effectiveness of adding enzalutamide vs standard non-steroidal antiandrogen drugs for patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer undergoing standard first-line therapy: a within-trial, secondary end-point analysis of the ENZAMET phase 3, international randomized trial (ANZUP 1304)
abstract: Background: The ENZAMET randomized trial demonstrated adding enzalutamide to testosterone suppression, compared with a less potent comparator, significantly improved overall and progression-free survival in men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC). This study evaluated cost-effectiveness of adding enzalutamide to standard therapy over 60 months. Methods: A within-trial cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted from an Australian health system perspective using prospectively collected, observed data from ENZAMET open-label, phase 3 RCT. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02446405, ANZCTR, ACTRN12614000110684, and EudraCT, 2014-003190-42. The analysis was conducted utilizing a data cut-off date of January 19, 2022, with a median follow-up of 68 months. Information on disease status, healthcare utilization, and health-related quality of life were extracted from trial records, linked Medicare claims and patient questionnaires. Costs were calculated in 2023 Australian dollars. EQ-5D-5L scores were converted to health utilities using a validated algorithm. Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were estimated by multiplying mean health utility with corresponding life-years accumulated. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses examined the effect of varying unit price of study drugs, per diem rates of hospital stays, benefits paid from Medicare claims, and health utility values on robustness of results. Data were assessed for missingness and imputation applied where relevant. Findings: Enzalutamide was associated with an additional AUD$127,262 per patient in healthcare costs, 0.24 life-years and 0.15 QALYs gained in the first 5 years, compared with non-steroidal antiandrogen therapy. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, (ICER) was AUD$543,880 per life-year gained and AUD$835,580 per QALY gained. Results were sensitive to the cost of study drug, with a purchase price of AUD$6.73 per tablet yielding an ICER that met the willingness-to-pay threshold of AUD$50,000 per QALY gained. Of note, hospitalizations were slightly higher in the enzalutamide group; as was use of musculoskeletal medicines, the latter indicating falls and fractures. Interpretation: Although Enzalutamide improves quality-adjusted survival for men with mHSPC, it is unlikely to be cost-effective. Long-term bone health management in survivors is an important clinical consideration. Funding: Astellas Pharma and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council.

title: The Lancet commission definition of clinical obesity: a multi-cohort cross-sectional analysis from early childhood to older age in seven high-income countries
abstract: Background The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission on Clinical Obesity established a consensus definition for clinical obesity (excess adiposity with clinical or laboratory evidence of adiposity-related sequelae). In contrast to body mass index (BMI)-based criteria, this new definition conceptualises obesity as a chronic disease to guide prevention and management. We sought to determine the age-specific cross-sectional prevalence of clinical and BMI-defined obesity from early childhood to older age. Methods We analysed 11 population-derived childhood and adult cohorts in Australia, Canada, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, UK, and US ( n = 786,557) from 1996 to 2023. Cross-sectional prevalence of BMI-defined (using Centres for Disease Control and Prevention cut-points) and clinical obesity was calculated for each age group across cohorts, stratified by sex and education level. Findings No cohort captured all diagnostic criteria for clinical obesity. Using available heterogeneous data spanning different epochs, the cross-sectional prevalence of clinical obesity (range 2.1–4.9%) was lower than BMI-defined obesity (7.0–10.8%) in childhood and adolescence, increased across adulthood, surpassed BMI-defined obesity prevalence in mid-to-late adulthood, and peaked at 65–74 years (52.0% vs. 34.4% for BMI-defined obesity). Clinical obesity prevalence was higher in men compared to women in early-to-mid adulthood (e.g. 18.6% vs. 13.9%, respectively at 35–44 years), and higher in women later in adulthood (e.g. 44.1% vs. 57.1%, respectively at 65–74 years). Clinical obesity was marginally less prevalent in the highest education group (range 1.3–48.2%) compared to the lowest (3.6–55.0%). Interpretation We provide population-level cross-sectional prevalence data on clinical obesity, which were largely consistent across diverse high-income settings. The findings highlight challenges in operationalising the Commission's conceptual definition in epidemiological studies using large-scale, incomplete and heterogeneous real-world data. Population data capturing all diagnostic criteria of clinical obesity are essential to further improve the understanding of the prevalence and translational implications of these definitions. Funding No study-specific funding to declare.

title: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli hyperimmune bovine colostrum for preventing travellers’ diarrhoea (TD): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
abstract: Background: (ETEC) is a leading cause of travellers' diarrhoea (TD). Hyperimmune bovine colostrum (HBC) containing ETEC specific antibodies has shown efficacy in controlled settings, but despite widespread use, real-world efficacy remains uncertain. Methods: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled superiority trial, US and UK military personnel and adult civilians (aged 18-70 years) travelling to TD-risk regions were randomised (1:1) to receive ETEC HBC (600 mg twice daily) or placebo, starting 2 days before arrival and continuing for 10-20 days while in the risk area. The primary outcome was TD, defined by standardised criteria. Stool smears collected during diarrhoeal episodes and at the end-of-prophylaxis were tested by PCR for pathogen attribution. ETEC-attributable TD was assessed as a secondary outcome. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04605783 and is complete. Findings: Between June 2, 2022, and April 29, 2025, 975 participants were enrolled and 850 were randomised to ETEC HBC (n = 425) or placebo (n = 425). Of these, 317 ETEC HBC and 323 placebo recipients were included in the primary efficacy analysis. TD occurred in 22.7% of ETEC HBC and 26.3% of placebo recipients (relative protective efficacy [PE] 13.7 [95% CI -13.4 to 34.31]), below the protocol-specified efficacy threshold of ≥35%. ETEC accounted for 17% of attributable TD cases, with frequent multi-organism detections. The difference in ETEC attributable TD between the groups was not statistically significant (12.1 vs. 21.5%; PE: 43.8 [-28.5 to 75.4]). Adverse events were rare and mild (ETEC HBC 2/320 vs. placebo 2/325). Both events in the ETEC HBC group (frequent urination, hives) resolved spontaneously. Interpretation: ETEC HBC did not significantly reduce overall TD risk, with interpretation of ETEC-specific efficacy constrained by limited power. Further research is warranted to determine whether broader ETEC antigenic coverage or multi-pathogen approaches can overcome the pathogen diversity and polymicrobial infections observed in field settings. Funding: Defense Health Agency.

title: Sex and weighting in abbreviated DASI-based perioperative risk prediction
abstract: We congratulate Wijeysundera and colleagues1 for this rigorous pooled analysis refining perioperative functional capacity assessment. Their findings show that the 12-item Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) provides modest incremental prognostic value and is best applied as a continuous, context-dependent measure rather than a binary threshold.

title: Authors' reply to “Sex and weighting in abbreviated DASI-based perioperative risk prediction”
abstract: We thank Ho and colleagues for their thoughtful comments1 on our analysis.2 We welcome the opportunity to address their questions regarding sex-related differences in the prognostic performance of the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI), the impact of item weighting on the performance of the modified four-item DASI (M-DASI-4Q),3 and the potential prognostic value of biological age.

title: Chronic pelvic and related genital pain in transgender and gender-diverse people: a scoping review
abstract: Background: Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) and related genital pain are disabling and multifaceted, but understudied in transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people. Methods: In this scoping review, we mapped evidence on prevalence, aetiology, assessment, and management across gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT), surgical, and community contexts. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) reporting guidance, we searched ten databases from database inception to 30 July 2025, supplemented by citation chasing, and including primary-data reports of duration-defined CPP (persistent or recurrent pelvic pain for at least three months) or related pelvic and genital pain within a broad chronic pain framework. The search protocol was registered prospectively on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/mk6cp). Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted published data. Findings: 24 reports representing 23 unique cohorts and 5527 TGD participants were included. Only one study explicitly estimated duration-defined CPP prevalence, reporting 17·7% among TGD adults assigned female at birth. Broader pelvic and genital pain outcomes ranged from 9·6% to 72·2% across five studies, but should not be interpreted as duration-defined CPP prevalence. Four non-mutually exclusive domains were identified: hormonal and tissue-mediated, pelvic floor and musculoskeletal, surgical and anatomical, and psychosocial and trauma-related. Assessment and diagnostic pathways were heterogeneous. Management evidence was very limited and derived almost entirely from observational studies, programme audits, and case reports; only one short randomised trial evaluated an intervention. Interpretation: Our findings support gender-affirming, multidisciplinary evaluation while highlighting the need for standardised CPP definitions, validated TGD-specific patient-reported measures, prospective cohorts, and adequately powered interventional trials. Funding: None.

title: Dose-dependent efficacy and renal safety of pemafibrate versus fenofibrate in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and hypertriglyceridemia: a multicenter randomized controlled, open label trial
abstract: Background No randomized controlled trial has directly compared the efficacy of pemafibrate to that of fenofibrate, or evaluated the dose–response relationship of pemafibrate in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Therefore, we compared the efficacy and safety of high- and low-dose pemafibrate versus fenofibrate over 48 weeks in patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia. Methods This multicenter, open-label, prospective, randomized controlled phase 4 trial (the PRESENT study) included 360 patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia at 29 sites in Japan between December 23, 2020, and March 31, 2026. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to high-dose pemafibrate (0.4 mg/day; PEM-H), low-dose pemafibrate (0.2 mg/day; PEM-L), or fenofibrate (53.3–106.6 mg/day; FENO) groups. The primary endpoint was change in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels at Week 24. Secondary endpoints included liver fibrosis markers, renal parameters, magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), and adverse events. The trial was registered in the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials on December 28, 2020 (jRCTs031200280). Findings At Week 24, PEM-H and PEM-L produced significantly greater ALT reductions than FENO (p < 0.001 and p=0.015, respectively). Exploratory comparison revealed greater reduction for PEM-H than PEM-L (p = 0.018, Holm adjustment), suggesting a dose-dependent effect. Higher baseline ALT levels and lean phenotypes were independently associated with ALT response. At Week 48, Mac-2 binding protein glycosylation isomer decreased significantly in PEM-H and PEM-L compared with a modest reduction in FENO (p < 0.001 and p < 0.001, respectively). MRE demonstrated significant decreases in liver stiffness in PEM-H and PEM-L compared with FENO (p < 0.05 and p=0.02, respectively). Percentage change in serum creatinine levels was lower in PEM-H and PEM-L than in FENO. No treatment-related serious adverse events were observed in any of the three groups. Interpretation Pemafibrate demonstrated greater reductions in ALT levels than fenofibrate, with a notable dose–response relationship and favorable safety profile, suggesting therapeutic potential for patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia. Funding This study was funded by the Kowa Company, Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan).

title: Adjuvant radiotherapy in FIGO stage III dMMR endometrial cancer: evidence and perspectives in the molecular era
abstract: Current guidelines incorporate chemo-immunotherapy for stage III-IV mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) endometrial cancer, but the evidence supporting omission of adjuvant radiotherapy remains insufficient. Given the pivotal role of pelvic radiotherapy in achieving durable locoregional control in high-risk endometrial cancer, and the lack of robust randomized evidence demonstrating equivalence of systemic therapy alone, the suggestion that EBRT may be safely omitted in the adjuvant treatment of dMMR high-risk disease warrants careful consideration. Importantly, PORTEC-3 (NCT00411138) included radiotherapy in both treatment groups and no immunotherapy, whereas in KEYNOTE-B21 (ENGOT-en11/GOG-3053, NCT04634877) radiotherapy was not randomized; neither trial therefore directly tested the safety of radiotherapy omission. In this Viewpoint, we review current evidence and unresolved questions in the adjuvant management of FIGO stage III dMMR endometrial cancer, with particular attention to the role of radiotherapy in the evolving chemo-immunotherapy era. While our discussion is intentionally focused on dMMR disease, many of the broader considerations regarding the interpretation of emerging evidence and the preservation of effective locoregional treatment are not exclusive to this molecular subgroup. Ongoing trials, including NRG-GY020 (NCT04214067) and the RAINBO MMRd-GREEN trial (ENGOT-en14/GREEN, NCT05255653), are expected to define the optimal integration of immunotherapy and adjuvant radiotherapy in molecularly stratified populations. Beyond survival, locoregional control, recurrence burden, and quality of life remain clinically meaningful endpoints. Future randomized trials should evaluate radiotherapy as an independent treatment variable within molecularly stratified populations, incorporating not only survival but also patterns of failure and patient-reported outcomes. Until such data become available, treatment de-escalation strategies should be adopted with caution.

title: Safety and tolerability of elinzanetant: a pooled analysis from four randomized clinical trials
abstract: Background: Elinzanetant is a dual neurokinin (NK)-1 and NK-3 receptor antagonist approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS) associated with menopause, or those caused by adjuvant endocrine therapy for breast cancer treatment. Methods: In this pooled safety analysis, safety data were pooled from four randomized, placebo-controlled studies: the phase IIb SWITCH-1 trial (2018-2019) and phase III OASIS-1-3 trials (2021-2024). All four studies were multicentre, multinational, double-blind trials that included postmenopausal women aged 40-65 years experiencing moderate-to-severe VMS due to natural or surgical menopause. Data were analysed exploratively. Assessments included frequency of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) over 12 and 52 weeks, and exposure-adjusted incidence rates (EAIRs, with 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) over 52 weeks. EAIRs were calculated by weighting event counts against total exposure time (person-years) across studies. Additionally, liver safety and incidence of neoplasms were evaluated. Findings: The 12-week pooled safety analysis set included 1519 participants: 765 participants in the elinzanetant 120 mg group and 754 participants in the placebo group. The 52-week pooled safety analysis set included 1113 participants in the elinzanetant 120 mg group and 754 participants in the placebo group. TEAEs occurred in 50·8% and 43·2% of participants in the elinzanetant 120 mg and the placebo groups, respectively, over 12 weeks; EAIRs were 196·61 (95% CI 181·33-213·18) and 209·00 (95% CI: 188·96-231·15) in the elinzanetant and placebo groups, respectively, over 52 weeks. The most common TEAEs reported with elinzanetant were headache, fatigue, and somnolence. Treatment discontinuation was low with elinzanetant (7·8%) but higher than placebo (3·6%) over 12 weeks; EAIRs were 14·95 (95% CI 11·99-18·62) and 10·96 (95% CI 7·87-15·27), respectively, over 52 weeks. There were no Hy's Law cases or indication of cholestatic injury. EAIRs of malignant tumors had overlapping CIs between treatment groups. No endometrial hyperplasia/malignancy was reported in either group. Interpretation: The overall safety profile of elinzanetant appeared favorable in 1113 women based on this exploratory pooled safety analysis. Future time-to-event analyses of TEAEs and real-world post-marketing data are warranted to better characterize the long-term safety profile of elinzanetant. Funding: Bayer.

title: Adalimumab versus placebo as add-on to standard therapy for non-infectious uveitis in the United Kingdom: the ASTUTE randomised controlled trial with treatment run-in
abstract: Background: Immune-mediated non-infectious uveitis (NIU) is a leading cause of blindness in high-income countries. Adalimumab is the only licensed non-corticosteroid drug for non-infectious intermediate, posterior or panuveitis. We evaluated the efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness of an adalimumab biosimilar as add-on therapy for a broad NIU population. Methods: This multicentre, placebo-controlled randomised trial recruited adults with sight-threatening or controlled NIU requiring oral prednisolone >5 mg/day from 18 UK NHS ophthalmology departments between 29 July 2021 and 7 June 2024. After a 16-week treatment run-in (TRI) with adalimumab, responders (prednisolone ≤5 mg/day, no active disease) were randomised 1:1 (parallel groups; concealed web-based allocation) to fortnightly subcutaneous 40 mg adalimumab (biosimilar) or placebo as add-on therapy; all but the trial statistician were masked. The primary outcome, time to treatment failure (TF; disease activity or prednisolone >5 mg/day), was analysed at 12 months by intention to treat. The health economic evaluation was pre-specified in the trial protocol; we estimated incremental cost per TF avoided, NHS perspective. Registered: ISRCTN31474800. Findings: 182 participants completed the TRI, 119 (65.4%) responded, and 115 were randomised (60 adalimumab, 55 placebo). At 12 months, 31.4% (adalimumab) and 59.0% (placebo) had experienced TF (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.23-0.75, p = 0.003). Among patients ineligible for NHS treatment (85%), the effect was similar (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.20-0.71, p = 0.003). Adverse events were similarly frequent; two were serious, one per group. Incremental cost was £2320 per TF avoided. Interpretation: Adalimumab added to standard care reduces treatment failure in NIU, including in patients with macular oedema, unilateral disease, and steroid-dependent inactive uveitis, and is affordable. Future work should identify complementary treatments for disease refractory to adalimumab. Funding: Health Technology Assessment Programme, National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR); Biogen International GmbH (Baar, Switzerland) provided the placebo for the trial.

title: EUSEM Congress 2026
Pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin for advanced biliary tract cancer: longer-term follow-up from the randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 KEYNOTE-966 trial
abstract: Background: At the final analysis of KEYNOTE-966 (median follow-up 25·6 months), pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin (pembrolizumab group) versus placebo plus gemcitabine and cisplatin (placebo group) provided a statistically significant, clinically meaningful improvement in overall survival without any new safety signals in participants with advanced biliary tract cancer. We report results from a median study follow-up of 36·6 months (∼3 years). Methods: intravenously on days 1 and 8 of every 3-week cycle. Randomisation was done using a central interactive voice-response system and stratified by geographical region, disease status, and site of origin in block sizes of four. The primary endpoint of overall survival was evaluated in the intention-to-treat population (all participants randomly assigned to a treatment). Safety was evaluated in the as-treated population, comprising all participants who received at least one dose of study treatment. As the primary endpoint was met at the final analysis, updated data are reported without p values. This study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04003636. Findings: Between Oct 4, 2019, and June 8, 2021, 1069 participants were randomly assigned to the pembrolizumab group (n = 533) or the placebo group (n = 536). Median follow-up at data cutoff (Nov 14, 2023) was 36·6 months (IQR 32·7-41·4). The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0·86 (95% CI, 0·75-0·98) with pembrolizumab versus placebo; estimated 36-month overall survival rates were 13% (95% CI, 11-17) in the pembrolizumab group and 11% (95% CI, 8-14) in the placebo group. Grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 370 (70%) of 529 participants in the pembrolizumab group and 367 (69%) of 534 participants in the placebo group. No new treatment-related deaths occurred since the final analysis. Interpretation: With extended follow-up, the survival benefit of pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine and cisplatin observed at the final analysis persists with approximately 3 years of follow-up, with no new safety signals among participants with previously untreated metastatic or unresectable biliary tract cancer. Funding: Merck Sharp & Dohme LLC, a subsidiary of Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA.

title: Generalisability of an adult-trained AI model to paediatric coeliac disease diagnosis: a multicentre external validation study
abstract: Background: Coeliac disease diagnosis on duodenal biopsies is limited by interobserver variability. We have previously demonstrated pathologist-level performance with our artificial intelligence (AI) model for the histopathological diagnosis of adult coeliac disease, but not in paediatric practice. As paediatric coeliac disease screening programmes expand internationally, accurate and scalable diagnostic tools are needed. We investigated whether an AI model trained exclusively on adult whole-slide images (WSIs) can generalise to paediatric coeliac disease diagnosis across independent centres. Methods: A training and validation dataset of 9958 WSIs from 8421 adult patients (961 coeliac disease; collected Jan 1, 2014, to March 31, 2025) from five centres was used to develop an ensemble of multiple-instance learning models using features from a foundation model. Testing was performed on 708 consecutive paediatric patients (86 with coeliac disease) from two centres (Edinburgh and Southampton) not included in training. Model calibration was assessed, and probability outputs were grouped into clinically interpretable categories. Findings: In adult cross-validation, the AI model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 99.1% (95% CI 98.9-99.4), sensitivity of 89.3% (87.2-91.1), specificity of 98.8% (98.5-99.0), and negative predictive value (NPV) of 98.6% (98.3-98.9). On testing (paediatric) datasets, performance remained high (AUC 98.8%, 95% CI 98.2-99.4; sensitivity 80.2%, 70.6-87.3; specificity 98.4%, 97.1-99.1; NPV 97.3%, 95.7-98.3). Restricting analysis to predictions outside the intermediate-probability range (predicted coeliac disease probability <10% or ≥65%; 604 [85.3%] of 708 cases) improved sensitivity to 100% (95% CI 93.7-100.0) and specificity to 98.7% (97.4-99.4). No misclassifications were observed among high-confidence predictions (<2% or ≥85%; 467 [66.0%] of 708 cases). The expected calibration error was 0.03. Performance improved significantly when biopsies from both duodenal sites (bulb [D1] and descending [D2/3]) were considered. Interpretation: Our AI model, trained on adult biopsies, generalises to paediatric coeliac disease diagnosis across centres and scanner platforms. Well calibrated probability outputs provide clinically interpretable measures of diagnostic confidence and could support safe identification of coeliac disease-negative biopsies within defined thresholds. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying adult-derived AI models in paediatric populations and reinforce the importance of multi-site (D1 & D2) biopsy sampling. Funding: The National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Efficacy and safety of temporary selective portal vein embolization before major hepatectomy (EMBORES): a phase 2 trial
abstract: Background: Portal vein embolization (PVE) is routinely used before major hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy of the future liver remnant (FLR) and reduce post-hepatectomy liver failure. Conventional PVE relies on permanent embolic agents, resulting in irreversible portal occlusion, which may be associated with complications and may limit subsequent therapeutic options in patients who do not ultimately undergo resection. Whether transient portal deprivation alone can induce clinically relevant liver regeneration remains unknown. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of temporary selective PVE using an absorbable gelatin agent. Methods: EMBORES was a multicenter prospective single-arm phase II trial conducted in six French hepatobiliary centers. Between May 3, 2018, and May 3, 2021, adult patients requiring major hepatectomy and preoperative PVE were included. Selective portal branches were embolized using powdered absorbable gelatin sponge. The primary endpoint was FLR hypertrophy assessed by computed tomography (CT) volumetry 4-6 weeks after PVE. Secondary endpoints included feasibility, morbidity, portal vein recanalization, and surgical outcomes. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02945059. Findings: 34 patients were enrolled and 32 underwent temporary PVE. Mean age was 63.4 years (standard deviation [SD] 8.9), and colorectal liver metastases accounted for 18 (56%) of 32 indications. Technical success was achieved in all patients. One major complication occurred (1 [3.1%] of 32 patients), while liver function remained preserved. Complete and partial portal vein recanalization were observed in 17 (53%) and 9 (28%) of 32 patients, respectively. Mean FLR volume increased from 580 (SD 169) mL to 690 (SD 188) mL, corresponding to a mean hypertrophy ratio of 9.5% (SD 10.2). Five patients required repeat embolization using a permanent agent because of insufficient hypertrophy. Overall, 23 (71.8%) of 32 patients underwent major hepatectomy, with no postoperative mortality. Interpretation: Temporary PVE using an absorbable embolic agent is feasible, safe, and capable of inducing clinically meaningful liver hypertrophy before major hepatectomy, supporting the concept that transient portal vein occlusion may be sufficient to stimulate liver regeneration in selected patients. Funding: The EMBORES study was funded by the French Ministry of Health through a national hospital clinical research program grant awarded in 2015 (Programme Hospitalier de Recherche Clinique National, PHRC-15-15-0201).

title: Relative risk reduction is not enough: why cardiorenal trials should routinely report absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat
abstract: Cardiorenal outcome trials have transformed the management of cardiovascular and kidney disease, particularly through glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors. Treatment effects are commonly communicated using relative measures, including hazard ratios and relative risk reductions. Although essential for estimating treatment effects, these measures do not directly communicate the absolute magnitude of benefit experienced by patients. Absolute risk reduction (ARR) and number needed to treat (NNT) provide complementary information by incorporating underlying event risk and duration of follow-up. The distinction is clinically important. Similar relative treatment effects can produce substantially different absolute benefits depending on baseline risk, outcome definitions, follow-up duration, and study population characteristics. Conversely, a NNT from one trial should not be used to rank therapies across studies because differences in populations and endpoints strongly influence absolute event rates. For time-to-event outcomes, ARR should be estimated from cumulative event probabilities at a specified time point, preferably using appropriate survival methods. Hazard ratios reflect a lower estimated hazard over follow-up and should not be interpreted as equivalent to reductions in cumulative risk, and differences in annualized incidence rates should not be directly converted into conventional NNT estimates. We argue that relative and absolute measures should be presented together. Routine reporting of relative treatment effects, baseline event risks, ARR, and NNT, with a specified time horizon and method of estimation, would improve transparency and clinically meaningful interpretation. This approach would help clinicians, patients, guideline committees, and policymakers understand not only whether a therapy works, but also the magnitude of benefit that may reasonably be expected.

title: Weight loss and blood pressure lowering with GLP-1 receptor agonists and multi-hormone receptor modulators in overweight and obesity: a systematic review and meta-regression of phase 3 clinical trials
abstract: Background Obesity and hypertension frequently coexist, and weight-reduction is recommended as a core strategy for blood pressure (BP) management in adults with overweight or obesity. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and emerging multi-hormone receptor modulators (MHRMs) induce substantial weight loss alongside modest BP reductions. However, the extent to which weight-loss is associated with BP lowering across these therapies remains unclear. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of phase 3 randomized controlled trials evaluating GLP-1RAs and MHRMs in adults with overweight or obesity (PROSPERO: CRD420251146441). We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from 1946 to December 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Placebo-adjusted changes in body weight and BP at each trial's primary endpoint were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse-variance weighting. Meta-regression assessed the association between weight loss and BP reduction. Findings Thirty-seven trials including 50,171 participants were analysed. Thirty-six trials had low risk of bias across all domains. Across all trials, 50% of participants were females, 16% had type 2 diabetes and 57% had hypertension. Median treatment duration was 68 weeks. Mean placebo-adjusted weight loss was −10.1% (95% CI −11.3 to −9.0) accompanied by a −4.9 mmHg (95% CI −5.5 to −4.3) reduction in systolic BP. Between-trial meta-regression showed that 76% of the variance in systolic BP reduction was explained by differences in weight loss (R 2 = 0.76; P < 0.01), corresponding to a reduction of 0.37 mmHg (95% CI 0.28 to 0.45) per 1% change in body weight. Interpretation Across phase 3 trials of GLP-1RAs and MHRMs, greater weight loss was strongly associated with larger reductions in BP, supporting pharmacological weight-loss therapies as an adjunct strategy for BP management in obesity. Funding None.

title: Sex and disease differences in patients’ diagnostic experiences in autoimmune diseases: an international cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Females have higher rates of autoimmune disease and reported misdiagnoses. Our study uses patient-reported diagnostic data to capture, and compare between sexes and diseases, elements of the diagnostic journey not routinely documented in medical records. Methods In this international cross-sectional study, an online survey was used to capture data on the time from symptom onset and number of clinician consultations before achieving the autoimmune diagnosis, and rates and types of reported misdiagnoses. These were then compared between males and females (self-reported biological sex). The survey was co-designed, pre-tested, and approved by patients, charities and clinicians. It was made available internationally through an online survey platform between Dec 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025. Any individual aged 18 years or older reporting any autoimmune or rheumatic disease of likely inflammatory origin (e.g., polymyalgia rheumatica) confirmed in a clinical correspondence was eligible to participate. Patient-reported measures included: time to diagnosis and number of healthcare visits from symptom onset, and types of perceived misdiagnoses. Pearson Chi-squared tests and Bayesian regression models were used to compare males and females. Results were adjusted for potential confounders. Firth's penalised logistic regression model was used for disease group due to small numbers of males in some categories of misdiagnosis. This work is registered with the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/p4jgw/overview). Findings Of the 6607 participants with autoimmune diseases, most were female (91.2%), White (87.8%), and resided in the UK (69.7%). Females were significantly more likely than males to report longer delays to diagnosis from symptom onset, more visits to healthcare providers, and a higher proportion reported that their autoimmune disease had been attributed to psychiatric (43.3% vs. 32.7%; p < 0.001) and psychosomatic causes (33.9% vs. 21.5%; p < 0.001). While more males than females reported being misdiagnosed with another physical disease (47.6% vs. 43.5%), this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.131). Disease group was a significant predictor of perceived psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses with diseases with visible physical symptoms and/or more definitive biomarkers (e.g., Type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis) having lower rates of psychiatric/psychosomatic misdiagnoses. After adjusting for just disease group, females had significantly higher odds of reporting receiving mental health misdiagnoses (1.56, 95% CI 1.25–1.96; p < 0.001), and psychosomatic misdiagnoses (OR = 1.87, 95% CI 1.45–2.43; p < 0.001) than males. Following adjustment for age, disease group, continent, and household financial situation, females had significantly higher odds than males of psychiatric misdiagnoses (OR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.14–1.87; p=0.003) and psychosomatic misdiagnoses (OR = 1.74, 95% CI 1.31–2.32; p < 0.001). Interpretation In our survey sample, females with autoimmune diseases reported more challenging diagnostic journeys than males. Awareness of sex and disease differences in diagnostic experiences is essential for improving equality in care. The high number of reported psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses in both sexes may also reflect the challenges of interpreting presenting and evolving symptoms of autoimmunity. This is particularly relevant for primary care where most patients will initially present. This work is exploratory in nature and our findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future research is warranted into patients' and clinicians' perspectives on the causes of sex differences in diagnostic journeys and to design interventions to reduce diagnostic delays and psychiatric/psychosomatic misdiagnoses in autoimmune disease. Funding The Lupus Trust, Vasculitis UK, Lupus UK, SRUK, and Sjögren's UK.

title: Neighborhood disadvantages and longitudinal progression of multimorbidity among adult survivors of childhood cancer: a single-center St. Jude Lifetime Cohort Study in the U.S.
abstract: Background: The impact of cancer therapy on chronic health condition (CHC) burden in childhood cancer survivors is well-established; however, the role of neighborhood-level social determinants of health (SDOH) remains underexplored. Methods: In this single-center cohort study in the U.S., we analyzed 2508 survivors enrolled in the St. Jude Lifetime Cohort Study between 9/13/2007 and 4/20/2020, who were ≥5 years from diagnosis, ≥18 years of age, and had ≥2 clinical assessments. SDOH encompassed social vulnerability (Social Vulnerability Index) and environmental/healthcare access vulnerabilities (e.g., primary care physician [PCP] availability, food inaccessibility), categorized into quartiles. A total of 177 clinically assessed CHCs were aggregated into 48 CHC groups and a global burden. Multivariable logistic regressions examined associations between baseline SDOH and CHC progression from baseline to follow-up, adjusting for clinical and sociodemographic factors. Global CHC burden progression was the prespecified primary outcome; analyses of specific CHC groups and effect modification by personal socioeconomic status were exploratory. Findings: Survivors residing in the most vs. least vulnerable neighborhoods, characterized by low income (odds ratio [OR]: 1.83, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.36-2.46), limited PCP availability (OR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.03-1.64), and food inaccessibility (OR: 1.49, 95% CI: 1.08-2.07), had higher risks of global CHC burden progression. Living in SDOH-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher risks of new-onset/worsening of multiple CHC groups, including low education for peripheral nervous system disorders (OR: 2.69, 95% CI: 1.63-4.43), food inaccessibility for arrhythmias (OR: 4.36, 95% CI: 1.32-14.35), and poor walkability for abnormal glucose metabolism (OR: 4.60, 95% CI: 1.41-15.04). Among publicly insured survivors, limited PCP availability and poor walkability were associated with higher risk of peripheral musculoskeletal disorder (OR: 6.11, 95% CI: 2.33-16.04, OR: 7.37, 95% CI: 2.82-19.27). Interpretation: SDOH are associated with CHC severity progression among childhood cancer survivors, supporting multilevel social risk assessment in survivorship care and further evaluation of neighborhood-informed risk stratification. Funding: U.S. National Cancer Institute.

title: Corrigendum to “A methodology for determining dosing recommendations for anticancer drugs in patients with reduced kidney function”
abstract: Additional details on the management of conflicts of interest (COI) were requested post-publication to if clarify if COIs were actively managed during the consensus voting process, specifically for the drug-specific recommendations or was there reliance on anonymous voting to mitigate the risk.

title: Systematized scoping review of instruments for measuring adolescent digital technology use
abstract: Digital technology is a ubiquitous part of adolescent life, yet progress in understanding its implications for health and development is constrained by the lack of standardised, developmentally appropriate measurement tools. This systematized scoping review, conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, identifies and evaluates instruments used to measure adolescent digital technology use between 2014 and December 14 2025. Searches in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science yielded 533 peer-reviewed studies, from which 135 validated measurement instruments were identified. We extracted data on instrument characteristics and conducted a secondary search to evaluate psychometric properties using adapted COSMIN criteria. Most tools relied on self-reported frequency or duration of use, with 63% designed to detect problematic behaviours-such as social media addiction or gaming disorder-often using adult-derived clinical criteria. Fewer than 2% of instruments assessed positive or developmentally beneficial use. Tools frequently lacked adolescent-specific content, cultural adaptation, and validation across sociodemographic subgroups, and objective or multi-method measures were rare. Current measurement practices are heavily risk-focused and often insufficiently tailored to adolescents' developmental and sociocultural contexts. This review lays the foundation for WHO's efforts to develop more balanced, psychometrically robust, and culturally sensitive approaches to measuring adolescent digital technology use. Funding: None.

title: Sex work or male-with-male sexual activity and the risks of HIV and hepatitis C acquisition among people who inject drugs: a global systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background People who inject drugs (PWID) may engage in sexual behaviours that increase their HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) risk, including sex work and male-with-male sexual activity. We undertook a global systematic review to assess whether PWID who engage in these behaviours have higher HIV and HCV acquisition risks. Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO for studies among PWID published between 01/01/2000 and 09/06/2026 that included estimates of the association between male-with-male sex or sex work and our primary outcomes of HIV or HCV incidence. Studies that estimated incidence by longitudinally re-testing people at risk of infection or by using assays for recent infection were eligible for inclusion. We also contacted authors for unpublished estimates. We pooled estimates using random-effects meta-analysis. We used I 2 to assess heterogeneity, and we used Egger's test to assess publication asymmetry. This review is registered with Prospero (CRD42020220884). Findings We included 57 studies comprising 164 estimates. Among men, recent male-with-male sex was associated with higher HIV acquisition (pooled incidence rate ratio (IRR):2.35; 95% CI: 1.51–3.66; I 2 : 51%).) but not HCV (IRR: 1.28; 95% CI: 0.95–1.72; I 2 : 21%). Recent sex work had a 1.72-fold (95% CI: 1.30–2.28; I 2 : 65%) and 1.59-fold (95% CI: 1.29–1.96; I 2 : 60%) higher HIV and HCV acquisition risk among all PWID, respectively. When stratified, sex work was associated with higher HIV acquisition among women (IRR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.44–3.68; I 2 : 68%) but not men (IRR: 1.43; 95% CI: 0.92–2.22; I 2 : 51%), and was associated with HCV acquisition among men (IRR: 1.51; 95% CI: 1.22–1.87; I 2 : 0%), but not women (IRR: 1.26; 95% CI: 0.90–1.77; I 2 : 55%). For lifetime behaviours, only male-with-male sex was associated with HIV acquisition (IRR: 2.44; 95% CI: 1.18–5.02; I 2 = 87%). Results from Egger's tests did not provide evidence of asymmetry bias for our pooled estimates, while I 2 measures suggested considerable heterogeneity for many outcomes. Interpretation PWID who also engage in sex work or male-with-male sex were found to have higher HIV or HCV acquisition risks. Future research should aim to understand the mechanisms driving these associations. Funding Medical Research Council Greater Western Four Partnership Doctoral Training Partnership, Wellcome Trust, Canadian Institutes of Health Research and Medical Research Council.

title: Promoting equitable cancer care: learnings from the development of the Optimal Care Pathway for people living in rural and remote areas with cancer
abstract: Cancer care pathways outline best practice cancer care, bringing a focus on equity, and adherence is associated with better outcomes. They are often embedded in cancer international policies, providing a mechanism by which cancer and equity outcomes can be measured and achieved. In Australia, Optimal Care Pathways are nationally endorsed pathways for the delivery of quality, safe cancer care, and are a cornerstone of the Australian Cancer Plan—Australia's first national cancer control plan. This Viewpoint describes the learnings and recommendations from the development of an Optimal Care Pathway; specifically, the Optimal care pathway for people living in rural and remote areas with cancer. The development of cancer care pathways provides opportunity to ensure diversity in expertise, representation from those whom the pathway intends to serve, adoption of inclusive definitions and dedicated involvement of people with a lived experience of cancer. As cancer plans focus on equity, attention must be paid to how cancer care pathways are produced, resourced and enacted, and the recommendations presented support these equity goals.

title: The effects of the arts and arts therapies on mental health outcomes of children and young people: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background There is growing evidence on the positive effects of the arts and arts therapies for mental health (MH) outcomes. This review aims to fill a research gap by establishing the evidence on the effects of arts-based interventions on selected MH outcomes for children and young people (CYP). Methods Our systematic review and meta-analysis included randomised controlled trials with CYP aged 5–24 years receiving any type of arts-based intervention. Five databases (CINAHL, Embase.com, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between 1/1/2005 and 18/5/2025. Two reviewers independently screened all records and assessed risk-of-bias using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2) and certainty using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE). Data were initially extracted using the AI-assisted review tool Elicit and independently verified by two reviewers. All data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, and effect estimates for MH outcomes are summarised as Standardised Mean Differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with pre-specified subgroup and sensitivity analyses conducted to explore possible sources of inconsistency. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251015352). Findings One hundred trials across 29 countries involving CYP aged 5–24 years with a range of health conditions, alongside healthy populations, were included in this review. Based on studies with some concerns or high risk-of-bias, arts-based interventions were found to reduce individuals' depression (1.06 SMD lower [95% CI 0.45–1.67, n=1655, I 2 = 97%]), anxiety (0.75 SMD lower [95% CI 0.57–0.94, n=3898, I 2 = 87%]), and increase individuals' wellbeing (0.53 SMD higher [95% CI 0.26–0.80, n=538, I 2 = 49%]) and quality of life (0.54 SMD higher [95% CI 0.25–0.83, n=441, I 2 = 53%]) on average post-intervention. Certainty of results relating to wellbeing and quality of life was low due to imprecision and concerns about risk of bias, and very low for depression and anxiety due to additional inconsistency associated with high heterogeneity. Findings relating to anxiety were further supported by biomarker data (blood pressure and heart rate) with moderate certainty. Interpretation This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis of evidence from randomised controlled trials assessing the effects of a wide variety arts-based interventions on the mental health of CYP. Although the strength of any conclusions is limited by heterogeneity, imprecision and bias of the studies assessed, average effects were similar to those typically reported for established non-arts-based psychosocial interventions, including talking therapies. These findings advance our understanding of arts-based therapeutic strategies for CYP's MH. Further high-quality trials, with larger sample sizes and standardised outcome measures and timepoints, are needed to improve the certainty of evidence in this area. Funding UKRI.

title: Drug coated balloons versus drug eluting stents for de novo coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
abstract: Background Drug coated balloon (DCB) only percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has an established evidence base in small vessel de novo disease, but recent randomised studies have investigated its use across a broader spectrum of coronary disease. We systematically reviewed randomised evidence comparing DCB with drug eluting stent (DES) PCI for de novo coronary disease. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in line with the PRISMA statement. PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were systematically searched from inception until 30th May 2026 for randomised trials comparing DCB with DES PCI for de novo coronary disease. Principal outcomes were cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction (MI) and revascularisation. Random-effects models generated odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and publication bias by visual inspection of funnel plots. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB2. This study was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251167202). Findings Ten RCTs including 7832 patients were identified. There was no significant difference between DCB and DES in cardiovascular death [OR 1.06 (0.75–1.49), p=0.76, I 2 = 0%] or MI [OR: 1.02 (0.76–1.36), p=0.91, I 2 = 0%]. These findings remained consistent after excluding small-vessel-only trials. Revascularisation did not differ across all trials [OR 1.39 (0.88, 2.20), p=0.16, I 2 = 57%] but was higher with DCB after excluding small-vessel-only trials [OR 1.84 (1.06–3.19), p=0.03, I 2 = 54%]. This finding was sensitive to exclusion of REC-CAGEFREE I. Visual inspection of funnel plots did not suggest substantial publication bias. Interpretation DCB and DES strategies had comparable rates of cardiovascular death and MI across the studied de novo coronary populations. The higher revascularisation rates observed after excluding small-vessel-only trials requires cautious interpretation given between-study heterogeneity and sensitivity to one trial. Further adequately powered RCTs with longer follow-up are required to establish the efficacy of DCB strategies in large vessels and more complex coronary lesions. Funding No funding was received for this study.

title: A multimodal digital NeuroMarker platform with composite and domain-level validity for identification of mild cognitive impairment: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a clinically heterogeneous syndrome that can represent an early manifestation of neurodegenerative disease. Diagnosis relies on assessments that are difficult to scale, leaving many individuals unidentified. Methods In this cross-sectional study conducted in the United States, Australia, and Spain between May 2022 and October 2024, 638 adults aged ≥ 50 years were classified as cognitively unimpaired (CU; n=441) or MCI (n = 197) using Petersen/NIA-AA criteria. Participants completed a self-administered, tablet-based assessment (Altoida NeuroMarker Platform) integrating motor, speech, and augmented reality tasks. An XGBoost classifier was trained to distinguish CU from MCI. Diagnostic performance, test-retest reliability, and convergent validity were evaluated. Findings Median assessment time was 13.8 min. Participants reported comfort with digital technology (67%), willingness to engage in cognitive screening (90%), and positive usability. Altoida's NeuroMarker differentiated MCI with ROC-AUC 0.90, 95% CI 0.88–0.92 and comparable performance in an independent cohort (ROC-AUC 0.87, 95% CI 0.80–0.93; n=75). Cognitive composite and domain scores were lower in MCI than in CU. Classifier agreement across repeated assessments was κ = 0.60, and reliability of composite and domain scores was moderate-to-good (ICC 0.55–0.80). The composite score correlated with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) ( r s = 0.40, p < 0.001) and Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) Total Index ( r s = 0.58, p < 0.001). The platform also showed convergent validity of cognitive domains (| r s | = 0.27–0.50, p < 0.001). Interpretation A brief, self-administered multimodal assessment identified clinically adjudicated MCI and demonstrated convergent validity, test-retest reliability, and consistent performance in an independent cohort. Prospective studies should evaluate its implementation in real-world workflows. Funding Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation; Altoida Inc.

title: Culturally adapted psychoeducation for bipolar disorder: a multicentre, assessor-masked, randomised controlled trial
abstract: Background: Adjunctive psychoeducation can reduce recurrence of mood episodes in bipolar disorder (BD), but evidence from low-resource settings is scarce. We evaluated whether culturally adapted psychoeducation (CaPE) plus treatment-as-usual (TAU) prolongs time to recurrence in adults with BD in remission in Pakistan, a lower-middle-income country. Methods: In this multi-centre, assessor-masked randomised controlled trial, adults with remitted bipolar I or II disorder at seven urban centres in Pakistan were randomly assigned to CaPE plus TAU or TAU alone. CaPE comprised 12 weekly individual sessions delivered by master's-level psychologists. The primary outcome was time to recurrence of any mood episode over 48 weeks, assessed with the Longitudinal Interval Follow-up Evaluation. Secondary outcomes included recurrence of depressive and manic/hypomanic episodes and clinical and quality-of-life measures. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05223959). Findings: Between June 2022 and March 2025, 303 participants were randomly assigned (148 TAU, 155 CaPE plus TAU); 12-month data were available for 284 of 303 (93.7%). Over 48 weeks, CaPE prolonged time to recurrence of any mood episode versus TAU (adjusted hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.42-0.69; p < 0.001). At 12 months, CaPE improved recovery (measured with the Bipolar Recovery Questionnaire, on which higher scores indicate greater recovery; adjusted difference 144.8, 95% CI 51.5-238.1; p = 0.002), knowledge and attitudes (78.2, 22.6-133.8; p = 0.006), medication adherence (-0.4, -0.8 to -0.1; p = 0.013), and depressive symptoms (-5.3, -7.8 to -2.7; p < 0.0001). All adjusted estimates account for age, sex assigned at birth, marital status, weeks since diagnosis, and weeks in treatment. Interpretation: Individual culturally adapted psychoeducation added to routine care reduced recurrence risk and improved clinical outcomes in Pakistani adults with BD, and could optimise maintenance treatment in Pakistan and other low-resource settings. Funding: Canadian Institutes of Health Research.
